## 5.3 Timeout settings (verdane_gh4_manual, pp. 23–24)
Timeouts protect the ventilation equipment when a command is sent but the expected reaction does not follow. The controller starts a timer each time it sends a command to a vent actuator and checks the result when the timer runs out. Verdane GH-4 Operator Manual - page 23 If a vent actuator does not report its end position within 312 seconds, the controller stops the motor and raises the travel alarm. Long ridge vents on older houses can be slow, especially in cold weather when the gear grease is stiff. If the travel alarm appears regularly on a healthy vent, check the actuator's end switches before changing anything in the settings. A separate storm timeout applies when the wind sensor triggers a forced close. In that case the controller keeps driving the actuator toward closed for as long as the storm condition lasts and repeats the command every two minutes. The timeout value can be changed by the installer in Menu > Ventilation > Settings > Timing. Raising it hides real faults for longer, so it should only be changed after the cause of repeated alarms has been understood. The value in use is printed on the module's settings report. Every timeout event is counted. The counters for each vent actuator are shown in Menu > Ventilation > Service > Statistics and can help to find a device that is slowly wearing out: a device whose counter rises week after week usually needs attention before it fails completely. Verdane GH-4 Operator Manual - page 24

## 5 Ventilation module 5.1 Overview (verdane_gh4_manual, pp. 21–22)
The ventilation module opens and closes the ridge and side vents with motorised vent actuators to control air temperature and humidity. It is one of the five control modules of the GH-4 and can be enabled or disabled in Menu > Ventilation > Settings without affecting the other modules. Up to eight vent groups can be configured. Each group is driven by one or more vent actuators that move together and report their position as a percentage, from 0 % (closed) to 100 % (fully open). The module reads the inside air temperature and humidity, the outside temperature, and the wind speed and direction from the weather mast. Wind and rain always take priority over temperature: a vent that faces into a strong wind is closed even if the greenhouse is too warm. All ventilation settings are found under Menu > Ventilation. Settings that could damage equipment are only visible after the installer code has been entered, and every change is written to the event log together with the user who made it. • Menu > Ventilation > Status shows the live state of all vent actuators and wind sensors. • Menu > Ventilation > Settings holds the targets, limits and timing values described in this chapter. Verdane GH-4 Operator Manual - page 21 • Menu > Ventilation > Service is used for manual operation and calibration. The status page shows one line per device. For each vent actuator it lists the commanded state, the reported state and the time of the last change; for each wind sensor it lists the current reading, the reading one hour ago and the date of the last calibration. A device that has not reported for more than a minute is shown in grey. When the ventilation module is disabled, all its outputs are switched to their safe state and its alarms are suppressed. The module's settings and schedules are kept, so it can be enabled again later without being set up from scratch.

## 7.3 Timeout settings (verdane_gh4_manual, pp. 39–40)
Timeouts protect the heating equipment when a command is sent but the expected reaction does not follow. The controller starts a timer each time it sends a command to a mixing valve and checks the result when the timer runs out. After the boiler is requested, it must report a supply temperature increase within 410 seconds; otherwise the request is cancelled and the burner alarm is raised. The time a boiler needs depends on its type and size. Condensing boilers usually react within two or three minutes; Verdane GH-4 Operator Manual - page 39 large biomass boilers can be much slower, and the timeout should then be raised by the installer. Mixing valves have no separate timeout. A valve that does not move is detected by comparing the pipe probe reading with the expected temperature after each change. The timeout value can be changed by the installer in Menu > Heating > Settings > Timing. Raising it hides real faults for longer, so it should only be changed after the cause of repeated alarms has been understood. The value in use is printed on the module's settings report. Every timeout event is counted. The counters for each mixing valve are shown in Menu > Heating > Service > Statistics and can help to find a device that is slowly wearing out: a device whose counter rises week after week usually needs attention before it fails completely.

## 8.3 Timeout settings (verdane_gh4_manual, pp. 46–47)
Timeouts protect the CO2 dosing equipment when a command is sent but the expected reaction does not follow. The controller starts a timer each time it sends a command to a dosing valve and checks the result when the timer runs out. After the dosing valve is opened, the CO2 reading must rise within 180 seconds; otherwise the valve is closed and dosing is suspended for the day. Verdane GH-4 Operator Manual - page 46 Sensors hung far from the distribution tubes react more slowly. If the dosing alarm appears in large compartments, move one CO2 sensor closer to a distribution branch before considering any change to the settings. Suspended dosing restarts automatically on the next day. It can also be restarted manually from the service page after the cause has been fixed. The timeout value can be changed by the installer in Menu > CO2 dosing > Settings > Timing. Raising it hides real faults for longer, so it should only be changed after the cause of repeated alarms has been understood. The value in use is printed on the module's settings report. Every timeout event is counted. The counters for each dosing valve are shown in Menu > CO2 dosing > Service > Statistics and can help to find a device that is slowly wearing out: a device whose counter rises week after week usually needs attention before it fails completely.

## 5.2 Schedules (verdane_gh4_manual, pp. 22–23)
The ventilation schedule tells the module what to aim for at each time of day. Schedules are edited on the controller or loaded from a configuration file on a USB stick, using the format shown below. Ventilation does not run on fixed times. Instead, the schedule defines day and night temperature targets and the times at which the targets change.
The vents open in proportion to how far the air temperature is above the active target. A morning purge can be scheduled to open all vents to 20 % for a few minutes after sunrise, which removes the humid night air before the crop starts transpiring.
During the change from the night target to the day target the controller ramps the target over 45 minutes instead of jumping, Verdane GH-4 Operator Manual - page 22 so the vents do not open suddenly. Example configuration entry:
[ventilation.group.ridge]
day_target = 24.0
night_target = 17.5
day_start = 07:15
night_start = 19:30
Schedule changes take effect at the start of the next control cycle, which runs every 30 seconds. Changes made through a USB file are shown on the screen for confirmation before they replace the active ventilation schedule. Up to four alternative ventilation schedules can be stored, for example one for summer, one for winter and two for special crops.

## 11.6 A device does not do what is expected (verdane_gh4_manual, p. 60)
Open the module's status page and compare the commanded state with the reported state. If they agree, the controller is doing what its settings ask for: check the targets, the active schedule set and any overrides such as storm protection or a boiler lock. If the commanded and reported states disagree, the problem is between the controller and the device. ## 8 CO2 dosing module 8.1 Overview (verdane_gh4_manual, p. 44)
The CO2 dosing module enriches the greenhouse air with carbon dioxide through a dosing valve, using either a gas tank or the boiler's cleaned flue gas. It is one of the five control modules of the GH-4 and can be enabled or disabled in Menu > CO2 dosing > Settings without affecting the other modules. The module has one main dosing valve and up to four distribution branches.
CO2 is measured in parts per million (ppm) by infrared CO2 sensors hung at crop height. Dosing only makes sense while the crop is photosynthesising and the vents are mostly closed. The module therefore reduces its target as the vents open and stops dosing completely at night. All CO2 dosing settings are found under Menu > CO2 dosing.
Settings that could damage equipment are only visible after the installer code has been entered, and every change is written to the event log together with the user who made it. • Menu > CO2 dosing > Status shows the live state of all dosing valves and CO2 sensors. • Menu > CO2 dosing > Settings holds the targets, limits and timing values described in this chapter.

## 6.6 Error codes (verdane_gh4_manual, p. 35)
Errors of the lighting module start with E-L. The code is shown in the alarm list together with the time at which the error first appeared and the device it belongs to.

## 4.5 Calibration (verdane_gh4_manual, p. 18)
Sensor readings drift slowly over time, and a drifting flow sensor makes the irrigation module react to values that are not real. Regular calibration keeps the readings trustworthy. Calibrate each flow sensor every 23 days, and again after any pipe work upstream of the sensor. Calibration procedure: • Open the zone valve manually from Menu > Irrigation > Service. • Collect the outflow of one dripper line in a measuring container for exactly one minute. • Enter the measured volume; the controller computes the new sensor factor. • Repeat for each zone and close the service page to resume the schedule. The date of the last calibration is stored for every flow sensor. When a calibration is due, a reminder appears in the maintenance list on the home screen; the module keeps working normally until the calibration is done. If a calibration gives a correction that is much larger than the previous one, clean the flow sensor and repeat the procedure before accepting it. A large jump is more often caused by dirt or a mistake during the procedure than by the sensor itself. Verdane GH-4 Operator Manual - page 18

## 4 Irrigation module 4.1 Overview (verdane_gh4_manual, pp. 13–14)
The irrigation module delivers water and dissolved nutrients to up to sixteen growing zones through solenoid zone valves fed by a single main pump. It is one of the five control modules of the GH-4 and can be enabled or disabled in Menu > Irrigation > Settings without affecting the other modules. Each zone has its own valve, an optional soil moisture probe and a flow sensor mounted on the zone's supply line. The main pump only runs while at least one zone valve is open, so a closed system never builds up pressure against the pump. Fertigation is handled by the same module. When a nutrient recipe is assigned to a zone, the injector doses the stock solution into the supply line while the zone valve is open, and the conductivity reading of the drain water is logged after each cycle. All irrigation settings are found under Menu > Irrigation. Settings that could damage equipment are only visible after the installer code has been entered, and every change is written to the event log together with the user who made it. • Menu > Irrigation > Status shows the live state of all zone valves and flow sensors. • Menu > Irrigation > Settings holds the targets, limits and timing values described in this chapter. Verdane GH-4 Operator Manual - page 13 • Menu > Irrigation > Service is used for manual operation and calibration. The status page shows one line per device. For each zone valve it lists the commanded state, the reported state and the time of the last change; for each flow sensor it lists the current reading, the reading one hour ago and the date of the last calibration. A device that has not reported for more than a minute is shown in grey. When the irrigation module is disabled, all its outputs are switched to their safe state and its alarms are suppressed. The module's settings and schedules are kept, so it can be enabled again later without being set up from scratch.

## 4.3 Timeout settings (verdane_gh4_manual, p. 16)
Timeouts protect the irrigation equipment when a command is sent but the expected reaction does not follow. The controller starts a timer each time it sends a command to a zone valve and checks the result when the timer runs out. Each zone valve must confirm that water is flowing within 240 seconds of being opened; otherwise the zone is closed and marked as dry-run. The flow confirmation comes from the zone's flow sensor. A short delay is normal on long supply lines, because the line has to fill before the sensor registers a steady flow. Lines longer than 60 metres may need a booster pump rather than a longer timeout. The pump also has a dry-running guard. If the main pump draws less than a quarter of its rated current for 20 seconds, it is switched off to protect the seals, whatever the zone timeouts are set to. The timeout value can be changed by the installer in Menu > Irrigation > Settings > Timing. Raising it hides real faults for longer, so it should only be changed after the cause of repeated alarms has been understood. The value in use is printed on the module's settings report. Every timeout event is counted. The counters for each zone valve are shown in Menu > Irrigation > Service > Statistics and can help to find a device that is slowly wearing out: a device whose counter rises week after week usually needs attention before it fails completely. Verdane GH-4 Operator Manual - page 16

## 8.5 Calibration (verdane_gh4_manual, pp. 48–49)
Sensor readings drift slowly over time, and a drifting CO2 sensor makes the CO2 dosing module react to values that are not real. Regular calibration keeps the readings trustworthy. Verdane GH-4 Operator Manual - page 48 Calibrate each CO2 sensor every 14 days with outside air, which the controller assumes to contain 420 ppm. Calibration procedure: • Stop dosing and open all vents fully for 20 minutes. • Carry the CO2 sensor outside or wait until the inside reading is steady. • Start the fresh-air calibration from Menu > CO2 dosing > Service. • The sensor is ready again after a two-minute warm-up. The date of the last calibration is stored for every CO2 sensor. When a calibration is due, a reminder appears in the maintenance list on the home screen; the module keeps working normally until the calibration is done. If a calibration gives a correction that is much larger than the previous one, clean the CO2 sensor and repeat the procedure before accepting it. A large jump is more often caused by dirt or a mistake during the procedure than by the sensor itself.

## 5.5 Calibration (verdane_gh4_manual, pp. 26–27)
Sensor readings drift slowly over time, and a drifting wind sensor makes the ventilation module react to values that are not real. Regular calibration keeps the readings trustworthy. Calibrate the wind sensor every 30 days by comparing it with a handheld anemometer at the mast. Calibration procedure: • Choose a calm moment with a steady light breeze. • Hold the handheld anemometer at the same height as the mast sensor for two minutes. • Enter the average reading in Menu > Ventilation > Service > Wind offset. • Run a full open-close cycle of each vent group to re-learn the travel limits. The date of the last calibration is stored for every wind sensor. When a calibration is due, a reminder appears in the maintenance list on the home screen; the module keeps working normally until the calibration is done. Verdane GH-4 Operator Manual - page 26 If a calibration gives a correction that is much larger than the previous one, clean the wind sensor and repeat the procedure before accepting it. A large jump is more often caused by dirt or a mistake during the procedure than by the sensor itself.

## 9.5 Sensor types (verdane_gh4_manual, p. 53)
The GH-4 works with the Verdane sensor family, which all use the same bus connector. The most common types are listed below. • Climate box: air temperature and humidity in a ventilated radiation shield, hung at crop height. • PAR sensor: light at the canopy, used by the lighting module. • CO2 sensor: infrared measurement of carbon dioxide in ppm. • Flow sensor: water flow in a zone supply line. • Pipe probe: contact temperature sensor for heating pipes. • Soil moisture probe: water content of the substrate. Sensors from other manufacturers can be connected through the analogue input box, which converts a 4-20 mA or 0-10 V signal into a bus reading. Their calibration has to be entered by hand.

## 3.3 Status LEDs (verdane_gh4_manual, p. 10)
The three LEDs above the screen are labelled POWER, STATUS and BUS. They show the state of the controller even when the screen is off. • POWER steady green: the controller is supplied and running. • STATUS steady green: all modules are working without alarms. • STATUS steady red: at least one alarm has not been acknowledged. • STATUS blinking red: a module has stopped because of an error. • BUS blinking green: data is being exchanged with the sensors. • BUS off: no sensor has answered for more than one minute. A blinking amber STATUS LED means that a firmware update has been downloaded and is waiting for confirmation on the panel. Control continues normally until the update is confirmed, as described in chapter 10.

## 11.2 Controller does not start (verdane_gh4_manual, p. 58)
If the screen and the POWER LED stay dark, check the mains fuse inside the housing and the circuit breaker that supplies the controller. If the POWER LED is on but the screen stays dark, the self-test may have found a fault. Wait two minutes; if the screen does not come on, switch the controller off for ten seconds and on again. While the controller is off, all relay outputs are open. Pumps, lamps and vents therefore stop in their current position, except for devices that have their own safety logic. Verdane GH-4 Operator Manual - page 58

## 3 Control panel overview 3.1 Front panel layout (verdane_gh4_manual, p. 9)
The front panel has a 7-inch touch screen in the centre, a jog wheel and four buttons on the right, and three status LEDs above the screen. The USB port for configuration files is behind a small cover at the bottom of the panel. The home screen shows the current state of every enabled module as a tile. Tapping a tile opens the status page of that module. The top bar shows the time, the active alarms and the maintenance reminders. The screen switches off after ten minutes without use and comes back on as soon as it is touched or a button is pressed.

## 11 Troubleshooting 11.1 General approach (verdane_gh4_manual, p. 58)
Most problems show up as an error code in the alarm list. Start with the code: the first letter after E- tells you the module, and the error code table in that module's chapter lists the meaning and the first action to take. If there is no error code, check the status page of the module that behaves unexpectedly. It shows the live readings, the active targets and the state of every output, which usually explains why the module does what it does. Before calling for help, note the controller's serial number, the firmware version from Menu > System > About, and the exact error code.

## 6.2 Schedules (verdane_gh4_manual, pp. 30–31)
The lighting schedule tells the module what to aim for at each time of day. Schedules are edited on the controller or loaded from a configuration file on a USB stick, using the format shown below. The lighting schedule sets the photoperiod window, the daily light integral target and the dimming limits. Inside the window, lamps are switched on whenever the controller predicts that the target will not be reached by natural light alone. The dusk cutoff is the latest time of day at which supplementary lamps may run; its default value is 21:40. After that time all circuits are switched off, even if the daily light integral has not been reached, so that the crop gets an uninterrupted dark period. A dawn start time works the same way at the beginning of the day. Short-day crops usually need both limits set carefully, Verdane GH-4 Operator Manual - page 30 because a single hour of extra lamp light in the evening can delay flowering. Example configuration entry:

[lighting.circuit.2]
dli_target = 14.0
max_dim = 85
contactor = "K2"

Schedule changes take effect at the start of the next control cycle, which runs every 30 seconds. Changes made through a USB file are shown on the screen for confirmation before they replace the active lighting schedule. Up to four alternative lighting schedules can be stored, for example one for summer, one for winter and two for special crops. Only one schedule is active at a time; switching between them is done in Menu > Lighting > Settings > Schedule set and is recorded in the event log. Times in schedules are local times. The controller follows the summer time change automatically if the time zone has been set in Menu > System > Date and time; otherwise all schedules shift by one hour twice a year.

## 12.2 Glossary (verdane_gh4_manual, p. 62)
• Daily light integral (DLI): the total amount of light a crop receives in one day, in moles per square metre. • Dead band: a small range around a target in which no action is taken, to avoid constant switching. • Fertigation: adding dissolved nutrients to irrigation water. • Installer code: the code that unlocks settings which can damage equipment. • PAR: photosynthetically active radiation, the part of light that plants use. • Photoperiod: the part of the day during which the crop receives light. • Termination switch: a switch on the last sensor of the bus that prevents signal reflections.

## 9 Sensors and networking 9.1 Sensor bus (verdane_gh4_manual, p. 51)
All sensors are connected to the controller through a single RS-485 sensor bus. Sensors are wired one after the other in a line; star wiring is not supported. The last sensor on the line must have its termination switch set to ON. Each sensor has a unique bus address printed on its label. The controller polls every sensor in turn, and the BUS LED blinks while this happens. See the technical specifications in chapter 12 for the limits of the bus. Long bus lines may need a repeater. Signs of a weak bus are sensors that drop out briefly in the alarm list or readings that freeze for a few minutes.

## 9.3 Network settings (verdane_gh4_manual, p. 52)
The controller has one Ethernet port. By default it gets its network address automatically. A fixed address can be set in Menu > Network > Address, which is recommended for sites with several controllers. Several controllers on the same network share weather data from a single weather mast. Set one controller as the weather master in Menu > Network > Weather; the others receive its readings every ten seconds. The network connection is not needed for control. If the network fails, every controller continues to work with its own sensors and its last known weather data.

## 2.4 First start-up (verdane_gh4_manual, pp. 6–7)
After switching on, the controller runs a self-test that takes about one minute. The start-up assistant then asks for the language, the date and time, the site coordinates and the installer code. The site coordinates are used to calculate sunrise and sunset, which several modules use in their schedules. Enter them as decimal degrees, for example 52.01 and 4.36. Verdane GH-4 Operator Manual - page 6 Finally, the assistant searches the sensor bus and lists all sensors it has found. Assign each sensor to a module and a location before leaving the assistant. Sensors can also be added later, as described in chapter 9.

## 2.5 Connecting the weather mast (verdane_gh4_manual, p. 7)
The weather mast carries the outside temperature and humidity sensor, the wind sensor, the wind direction vane, the rain sensor and an outside light sensor. It is connected to the sensor bus like any other sensor, through its own junction box at the foot of the mast. Mount the mast at least two metres above the highest ridge of the greenhouse and away from chimneys, trees and other buildings, which disturb the wind readings. The wind direction vane must be aligned to north during installation; the alignment mark is on the vane's base. Use the lightning protection module supplied with the mast. Without it, a nearby lightning strike can damage every device on the sensor bus, not only the mast sensors. Only one weather mast is needed per site. Sites with several controllers share the mast's readings over the network, as described in chapter 9.

## 6.5 Calibration (verdane_gh4_manual, p. 34)
Sensor readings drift slowly over time, and a drifting PAR sensor makes the lighting module react to values that are not real. Regular calibration keeps the readings trustworthy. Calibrate the PAR sensors every 60 days against the reference sensor supplied with the controller. Calibration procedure: • Switch all lighting circuits off and wait for a cloudless, steady light period. • Place the reference sensor next to the PAR sensor, at the same angle. • Read both values from Menu > Lighting > Service > Sensor check. • Accept the proposed correction factor if it lies between 0.85 and 1.15. The date of the last calibration is stored for every PAR sensor. When a calibration is due, a reminder appears in the maintenance list on the home screen; the module keeps working normally until the calibration is done. If a calibration gives a correction that is much larger than the previous one, clean the PAR sensor and repeat the procedure before accepting it. A large jump is more often caused by dirt or a mistake during the procedure than by the sensor itself. Verdane GH-4 Operator Manual - page 34

## 3.3 Status LEDs (verdane_gh4_manual, p. 10)
The three LEDs above the screen are labelled POWER, STATUS and BUS. They show the state of the controller even when the screen is off. • POWER steady green: the controller is supplied and running. • STATUS steady green: all modules are working without alarms. • STATUS steady red: at least one alarm has not been acknowledged. • STATUS blinking red: a module has stopped because of an error. • BUS blinking green: data is being exchanged with the sensors. • BUS off: no sensor has answered for more than one minute. A blinking amber STATUS LED means that a firmware update has been downloaded and is waiting for confirmation on the panel. Control continues normally until the update is confirmed, as described in chapter 10.

## 8.3 Timeout settings (verdane_gh4_manual, pp. 46–47)
Timeouts protect the CO2 dosing equipment when a command is sent but the expected reaction does not follow. The controller starts a timer each time it sends a command to a dosing valve and checks the result when the timer runs out. After the dosing valve is opened, the CO2 reading must rise within 180 seconds; otherwise the valve is closed and dosing is suspended for the day. Verdane GH-4 Operator Manual - page 46 Sensors hung far from the distribution tubes react more slowly. If the dosing alarm appears in large compartments, move one CO2 sensor closer to a distribution branch before considering any change to the settings. Suspended dosing restarts automatically on the next day. It can also be restarted manually from the service page after the cause has been fixed. The timeout value can be changed by the installer in Menu > CO2 dosing > Settings > Timing. Raising it hides real faults for longer, so it should only be changed after the cause of repeated alarms has been understood. The value in use is printed on the module's settings report. Every timeout event is counted. The counters for each dosing valve are shown in Menu > CO2 dosing > Service > Statistics and can help to find a device that is slowly wearing out: a device whose counter rises week after week usually needs attention before it fails completely.

## 7.3 Timeout settings (verdane_gh4_manual, pp. 39–40)
Timeouts protect the heating equipment when a command is sent but the expected reaction does not follow. The controller starts a timer each time it sends a command to a mixing valve and checks the result when the timer runs out. After the boiler is requested, it must report a supply temperature increase within 410 seconds; otherwise the request is cancelled and the burner alarm is raised. The time a boiler needs depends on its type and size. Condensing boilers usually react within two or three minutes; Verdane GH-4 Operator Manual - page 39 large biomass boilers can be much slower, and the timeout should then be raised by the installer. Mixing valves have no separate timeout. A valve that does not move is detected by comparing the pipe probe reading with the expected temperature after each change. The timeout value can be changed by the installer in Menu > Heating > Settings > Timing. Raising it hides real faults for longer, so it should only be changed after the cause of repeated alarms has been understood. The value in use is printed on the module's settings report. Every timeout event is counted. The counters for each mixing valve are shown in Menu > Heating > Service > Statistics and can help to find a device that is slowly wearing out: a device whose counter rises week after week usually needs attention before it fails completely.
